searchText: > It's not the hashing, it's the random disk access of over a billion different trie nodes. With low latency for both reads and writes. Yeah, implementations definitely should be storing code as a blob exactly as they do today; there's no reason at all to store code chunks the way we store storage slots So I read: https://blog.ethereum.org/2020/11/30/the-1x-files-code-merkleization/ but I don't understand "The Merkle proof needed for Stateless Ethereum is called a ‘witness’, and it attests to a state change by providing all of the unchanged intermediate hashes required to arrive at a new valid state root. " Can someone explain it to me or point me to an explanation? The part I'm struggling with is "...providing all of the unchanged intermediate hashes required to arrive at a new valid state root. " <@!334899589582946306> take this with a grain of salt since I haven't developed a serious understanding, but: I think the text is saying that the witness needs to include a proof of the state that the transaction reads, *prior* to the transaction having taken effect e.g. if the call reads pieces of state x, y, z, — then it'll be necessary to show a path through the merkle tree from those values all the way up to the root Ok Correct The witness is basically all of the pieces of the state that the transaction reads or writes, plus the merkle branches to those pieces Plus a witness of the code that forms the transaction? code is part of the state So you start at state A and execute function F and the result is state B. The witness is some proof that B is the correct state given F(A)? In order to be useful the witness must take less storage space than A + F? (Maybe + B?) actually you don't need B to be part of the witness You don't need to transmit F as F is just part of client code A + the merkle branch needs to be smaller than the entire code, but that's always true and by a lot Ok so the code merklization "problem" is what is the most efficient representation of the part of A that is the code for the transaction? right, that and the merkle branch Don't you need the inverse of the merkle proof of B to validate that the new head block's merkle root is correct? no because you can always generate that from B + the pre-state proof Given that the witnessing node needs to execute the code can you simply concat the opcode's (and maybe thier parameters) as you execute and take a hash of that as a proof? Does the pre-state proof include storage slots that are being set but not read then? Unless there are parts of the block that are written but not read; so for simplicity I think it's best to just count all writes as being reads So the pre-state proof will be invalid if the contract tries to write to anything that isn't included in the proof. What happens when F() changes and Fv1(A) != Fv2(A)? `F()` is consensus rules? > So the pre-state proof will be invalid if the contract tries to write to anything that isn't included in the proof. yes Both the reads and the writes need to be known to generate the proof though for the writes you technically don't need to include the leaves F can be modeled as unchanging F would only change in practice when there's a hard fork, but if that happens then it would be given to clients weeks in advance

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content:
> It's not the hashing, it's the random disk access of over a billion different trie nodes.  With low latency for both reads and writes.

Yeah, implementations definitely should be storing code as a blob exactly as they do today; there's no reason at all to store code chunks the way we store storage slots

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: So I read: https://blog.ethereum.org/2020/11/30/the-1x-files-code-merkleization/ but I don't understand "The Merkle proof needed for Stateless Ethereum is called a ‘witness’, and it attests to a state change by providing all of the unchanged intermediate hashes required to arrive at a new valid state root. "

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: Can someone explain it to me or point me to an explanation?

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: The part I'm struggling with is "...providing all of the unchanged intermediate hashes required to arrive at a new valid state root. "

excerpts.author: roboteddy
excerpts.content: <@!334899589582946306> take this with a grain of salt since I haven't developed a serious understanding, but: I think the text is saying that the witness needs to include a proof of the state that the transaction reads, *prior* to the transaction having taken effect

excerpts.author: roboteddy
excerpts.content: e.g. if the call reads pieces of state x, y, z, — then it'll be necessary to show a path through the merkle tree from those values all the way up to the root

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: Ok

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Correct

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: The witness is basically all of the pieces of the state that the transaction reads or writes, plus the merkle branches to those pieces

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: Plus a witness of the code that forms the transaction?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: code is part of the state

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: So you start at state A and execute function F and the result is state B. The witness is some proof that B is the correct state given F(A)?

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: In order to be useful the witness must take less storage space than A + F? (Maybe + B?)

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: actually you don't need B to be part of the witness

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: You don't need to transmit F as F is just part of client code

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: A + the merkle branch needs to be smaller than the entire code, but that's always true and by a lot

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: Ok so the code merklization "problem" is what is the most efficient representation of the part of A that is the code for the transaction?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: right, that and the merkle branch

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Don't you need the inverse of the merkle proof of B to validate that the new head block's merkle root is correct?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: no because you can always generate that from B + the pre-state proof

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: Given that the witnessing node needs to execute the code can you simply concat the opcode's (and maybe thier parameters) as you execute and take a hash of that as a proof?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Does the pre-state proof include storage slots that are being set but not read then?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Unless there are parts of the block that are written but not read; so for simplicity I think it's best to just count all writes as being reads

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: So the pre-state proof will be invalid if the contract tries to write to anything that isn't included in the proof.

excerpts.author: mrsimicsak
excerpts.content: What happens when F() changes and Fv1(A) != Fv2(A)?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: `F()` is consensus rules?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: > So the pre-state proof will be invalid if the contract tries to write to anything that isn't included in the proof.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: yes

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Both the reads and the writes need to be known to generate the proof

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: though for the writes you technically don't need to include the leaves

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: F can be modeled as unchanging

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: F would only change in practice when there's a hard fork, but if that happens then it would be given to clients weeks in advance
